text: I will model the fluid volume with the plenum centred on the engine valley: length along \(x\), bank-to-bank width along \(y\), and height along \(z\). Each runner will have a 30 mm straight horizontal lead followed by a 60 mm centreline-radius quarter bend, so its final centreline/port is exactly 90 mm outboard of the plenum wall; the port faces point downward. This interpretation is necessary because the bend alone accounts for 60 mm of the specified 90 mm offset. I’ll use a CAD union for the air volume, export face-derived patch STLs, then create a conformal tetrahedral OpenFOAM mesh with Gmsh. First I’m checking the installed build123d sweep interface before constructing the coarse shape.

The installed API supports algebra-mode sweeps. I’ll now build in metres, using the four longitudinal stations \(-112.5,-37.5,37.5,112.5\) mm (equal 75 mm pitch and equal 37.5 mm end margins, an explicit layout assumption). The throttle is an opening in the end face, not an added-length neck. I’ll construct the eight swept runner volumes and fuse them to the plenum, then inspect its topology and dimensions.

The first construction exposed that `CenterArc` is created in the global \(xy\)-plane, so those edges were disconnected from the \(yz\)-plane runner lead. I’ll replace it with a three-point `RadiusArc` whose points explicitly lie in the runner’s \(yz\) plane; this removes the angle-convention ambiguity and remains directly measurable.
I’ll now rebuild the coarse CAD volume with the corrected radius arcs and print the overall bounds and solid count.

The coarse topology is wrong: eight disconnected solids and bounds smaller than the requested plenum show that the box placement/origin assumption was invalid, so I will not proceed to meshing. I’ll inspect the primitive defaults and the individual sweep endpoints before correcting the CAD.

The diagnostics found two concrete issues: `Box` defaults to centred alignment, and a spatial `RadiusArc` chose an unintended support plane (visible as an erroneous change in \(x\)). I’ll use an explicitly oriented local plane for each `CenterArc`, and centre the plenum only in \(x,y\) with its base at \(z=0\).

The corrected fluid is one solid with the expected volume scale and path bounds. The lowest \(z=-20\) mm is the flat downward-facing port plane; its disk extends in \(x,y\), not below that plane. I’ll now tessellate and render the coarse volume from an oblique view before doing any patch extraction or meshing.

The rendered coarse solid shows the requested arrangement: four runners on each side, connected cleanly to the plenum, with flat downward port ends. Next I need a true circular throttle patch on the otherwise planar end wall (without inventing a neck length). I’ll inspect build123d’s face-splitting operation so the opening is topologically named rather than selected later by a bounding box.

I will classify the already-created boundary by analytic face type and known construction membership, not by bounding-box extremities. Before splitting the inlet disk, I’ll print every external face’s geometry class, area, centroid, and normal where defined; this verifies which faces are ports, runner walls, and plenum walls.

The topology is exactly separable: six planar plenum faces, eight cylindrical plus eight toroidal runner-wall faces, and eight circular port faces of area \(0.00113411\ \mathrm{m^2}\), matching a 38 mm diameter. I’ll split the negative-\(x\) plenum end face with a 70 mm circle created directly in that plane, yielding a named throttle disk and the complementary plenum-wall annulus.

The split setup is sound, but the algebraic `Circle` here is represented directly as a closed wire rather than a face with `outer_wire()`. I’ll inspect that object and pass its actual wire representation.
I’ll re-emit the split cell self-contained, including the inlet circle definition, so the final replay script has no dependency on the failed attempt.

I’ll move directly to a coarse conformal mesh. I’ll import the STEP volume into Gmsh, imprint the zero-thickness 70 mm inlet disk onto the end boundary, and inspect the resulting boundary surfaces before assigning physical patches.

The imprint worked: one volume with 31 external surfaces, including a 70 mm disk and its exact complementary end-wall face. I’ll now assign all eleven requested boundary names, generate a coarse first-order tetrahedral mesh at roughly 12 mm global size (with 7 mm on the 38 mm runners), write one STL per named patch from the actual Gmsh surface triangles, and convert the same mesh to OpenFOAM.

Reloading the BREP renumbered its entities, so hard-coded surface tags were invalid. I’ll classify the imported surfaces by their analytic geometry type and measured area/centroid, preserving the same construction-based identities, then mesh and export.

The coarse volume mesh now exists: 15,587 tetrahedra, all eleven requested named boundaries, and one air cell zone. The conversion’s “undefined faces” message commonly refers to faces assembled before Gmsh physical surfaces are matched, so I’ll run `checkMesh` now and inspect the final patch counts and mesh geometry rather than assume it is harmless.

`checkMesh` exited before reporting mesh statistics, despite the boundary file showing that all undefined faces were successfully assigned (there is no `defaultFaces` patch). I’ll rerun while capturing standard error as well, to identify the actual failure rather than infer it from the conversion warning.

The mesh itself was not rejected; OpenFOAM stopped because this newly created mesh-only case lacks mandatory empty `fvSchemes` and `fvSolution` dictionaries. I’ll add minimal valid dictionaries (no solver setup) and rerun the binding mesh check.

The exhaustive check reports one known finite-volume advisory for pure tetrahedral meshes: 269 boundary tetrahedra have too few internal neighbours for the determinant stencil. All topology, closure, cell volumes, non-orthogonality, and skewness pass. I’ll run the standard binding `checkMesh` and render the actual OpenFOAM mesh surface/edges to verify that the meshed geometry matches the CAD.

The standard `checkMesh` completed its topology and geometry sections, but the combined cell failed afterward because PyVista cannot read legacy Gmsh files without `meshio`. I’ll render the actual exported surface triangles instead (which are exactly the boundary elements used by the converted mesh) and preserve the standard check result separately.

The rendered coarse mesh preserves all eight bends and flat ports, with appropriate extra resolution on runner curvature. Before finishing, I’ll print the requested dimensions from the constructed geometry and mesh-derived patch areas, explicitly separating the two layout assumptions from user-specified dimensions.

The measurement cell encountered a harmless namespace collision: the later surface-classification list reused the name `plenum`. I’ll measure a freshly constructed reference box and retain the already-built fluid/patch geometry for all other values.

The manifold air volume and coarse conformal mesh are complete. Standard `checkMesh` reports **Mesh OK**: one connected region, 15,587 tetrahedra, 4,060 points, 11 boundary patches, maximum non-orthogonality 67.91°, maximum skewness 0.813, and near-zero boundary openness.

Measured values:
- Plenum: 300 × 120 × 80 mm.
- Throttle: 70.000 mm diameter.
- Eight runners: 38.000 mm diameter.
- Bends: 60.000 mm centreline radius and 90° turn.
- Port centreline offset: 90.000 mm from the plenum wall.
- Runner stations: −112.5, −37.5, 37.5, 112.5 mm; 75 mm equal pitch.

Assumptions made:
- A 30 mm horizontal straight lead precedes each 60 mm-radius bend, making the specified 90 mm wall-to-port-centre offset.
- “Evenly spaced” uses equal 37.5 mm end margins and 75 mm pitch.
- Left/right patch names correspond to negative/positive \(y\), respectively.

Eleven patch STLs are in `constant/triSurface`, and the OpenFOAM mesh is in `constant/polyMesh`. The exhaustive optional topology check additionally identifies 269 boundary tetrahedra with underdetermined finite-volume stencils; this is intrinsic to the coarse pure-tet boundary layer, while the standard binding check passes.
